newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge orders accused S. Korean spy released.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge orders accused S. Korean spy released.

text.p: A federal magistrate on Monday ordered the release of U.S. Navy computer specialist Robert Kim, who has been accused of passing secret documents to South Korea.

U.S. Magistrate W. Curtis Sewell rejected a request by federal government prosecutors that Kim, who was arrested last week at a diplomatic reception, be kept in jail while awaiting trial out of concerns that he might flee the country.

Sewell ordered the release of the Korean-born Kim, 56, an 18-year government employee who became a U.S. citizen in 1974, on a $200,000 bond, which was put up by four families from the church he attends.
The magistrate said the ruling would not take effect until Tuesday afternoon to give prosecutors a chance to appeal. Justice Department spokesman John Russell later said an appeal would be filed.
The ruling requires Kim and his wife to surrender their passports and Kim must restrict his travel to the Washington, D.C. area. He must also report regularly to court authorities.

Kim, who worked at a U.S. Navy intelligence facility, was charged last week with passing dozens of secret and top-secret documents since May to a South Korean agent, Capt. Dong-Il Baek, a naval attache at the South Korean embassy.

Sewell agreed with prosecutors that the evidence against Kim appeared "overwhelming" and that the offence could have "serious consequences," but concluded there was no indication Kim had any intention of fleeing the country.
He also noted that Kim had no prior criminal record.
After the court hearing, defence attorney James Clark told reporters Sewell made the right decision in freeing Kim.
"He has no place to go," Clark said, adding that South Korea would be highly unlikely to put its close U.S. ties at risk by offering Kim safe haven.

Clark said during the court hearing the case was unique in that Kim did not appear to jeopardise U.S. national security, that he received no money and that he had not been recruited by a foreign nation.
"Mr Kim did something very ill advised and very stupid," but he said South Korea, a close U.S. ally, would have received the classified documents later anyway.
He acknowledged that Kim had been to South Korea four times since 1990, but said the sole purpose had been to visit his elderly father.
Clark said FBI agents during the investigation knew that Kim had been mailing sensitive documents to Baek, even opening up the envelopes, but took no immediate "steps to curtail his activities."

Prosecutor Robert Chesnut told the judge a federal grand jury would take up the case next month and said it would consider bringing more serious espionage charges than the current charges, which carry a 10-year prison term.
"He has no reason to stay here," Chesnut said of Kim, who has relatives in South Korea. The prosecutor said Kim has an estimated $100,000 in credit card debt.
